name: Record Keeping & Financial Management

objectives.text: Explain why keeping accurate records of a project's activities, time, and money helps a person learn and make good decisions
Record the date, activity, and hours worked on a project in a simple daily log
Classify project transactions as income or expenses
Record basic income and expenses for a class or chapter project and calculate whether it made or lost money
Organize receipts, invoices, and pay stubs as documentation that supports each recorded transaction
Enter SAE hours, income, and expenses into AET or another agricultural record-keeping system
Implement a consistent record-keeping routine suited to a specific entrepreneurship, placement, or research SAE
Distinguish cash and non-cash transactions and operating and capital expenses in SAE records
Prepare beginning and ending inventories of current and noncurrent SAE assets
Record wages, hours, and non-cash compensation earned in a placement SAE
Calculate depreciation on SAE capital assets such as breeding livestock, equipment, and facilities
Prepare an SAE income statement and calculate net profit or loss for the year
Prepare an SAE balance sheet that shows assets, liabilities, and net worth
Compare the purposes of income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow statements and how often each is used to monitor an SAE
Explain how credit, loans, and interest affect SAE liabilities and profitability
Analyze an SAE budget against actual income and expenses to explain variances
Interpret SAE financial measures such as return on investment, labor efficiency, break-even price, and change in net worth
Evaluate the accuracy, completeness, and appropriateness of SAE records before submitting a proficiency award or FFA degree application
Explain the income tax and reporting obligations that apply to earnings from an SAE
Evaluate SAE financial records to justify a business decision such as expanding, reinvesting, or changing an enterprise

changes: Kept and reworded all six existing objectives, splitting the grade 10 and 12 items into distinct competencies (income statement, balance sheet, depreciation, financial measures such as labor efficiency). Added competencies for daily logs, income and expense classification, source documentation, inventories, cash and non-cash and capital transactions, placement wages, financial report comparison, credit and interest, budget variance analysis, tax obligations, and record-based decision making. SAE type selection, goal setting, and portfolio presentation were left to sibling sub-topics.
